meta.title: Did Gandhi really say Western civilization "would be a good idea"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No record before 1967 — nineteen years after Gandhi died — and even that first appearance is hedged narration on a TV documentary. The joke itself predates him: a 1923 magazine filler runs 'It's a good idea. Somebody ought to start it.'
meta.ogTitle: Did Gandhi really say Western civilization 'would be a good idea'?
meta.ogDescription: Asked what he thought of Western civilization, Gandhi supposedly replied 'I think it would be a good idea.' No record before 1967 — and the gag was already in print in 1923.

answer.label: No record before 1967 — the joke predates Gandhi
answer.sourceLine: The exchange — a reporter asks what he thinks of Western civilization; Gandhi replies that it would be a good idea — has no contemporaneous record. Gandhi died in January 1948; the earliest attribution we can date is January 1967, in newspaper coverage of a CBS documentary where the line was spoken by the narrator, and hedged even then: Gandhi “was reported to have answered.” The joke itself was already in print in 1923.

source.heading: What Gandhi actually said about Western civilization

docMeta.dd: January 1967 — press coverage of a CBS documentary
Narration, hedged: ‘was reported to have answered’
Life, 1923: ‘It’s a good idea. Somebody ought to start it.’

source.excerpt: This civilization is such that one has only to be patient and it will be self-destroyed. […] Civilization is not an incurable disease, but it should never be forgotten that the English people are at present afflicted by it.
trail: The earliest attribution located is January 1967, in a newspaper report on the CBS News special The Italians — where the anecdote is narration rather than footage, and the paper itself hedges with ‘was reported to have answered.’ It spread from there via a magazine reprint later that year Quote Investigator ↗.

The gag existed before Gandhi supposedly delivered it. Life ran it as filler in 1923 — ‘What’s your opinion of civilization?’ ‘It’s a good idea. Somebody ought to start it’ — and a 1925 newspaper carried a near-relative. A joke template in circulation is exactly what migrates onto a famous name the 1923 antecedent ↗.

Gandhi’s real verdict on Western civilization is on the record, in Hind Swaraj (1909), and it is far harsher than the quip — he calls it a disease that will destroy itself, and describes the English as presently afflicted by it Hind Swaraj ↗.
source.excerptNote: Gandhi in his own words, chapter VI. He did not think Western civilization had yet to start — he thought it was a sickness in progress. The witticism is gentler than anything he actually wrote.
source.rightsNote: Free to reuse. The apocryphal quip has no identified author and no rights holder. The 1923 Life antecedent is in the United States public domain, and Gandhi’s Hind Swaraj (1909) is public domain and published free by the Government of India. You may quote any of it — provided you do not present the quip as something Gandhi is recorded as saying. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Mahatma Gandhi
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Gandhi
author.metaLine: 1869–1948 · leader of the Indian independence movement
author.bio: Mohandas K. Gandhi (1869–1948) was a genuine and radical critic of Western civilization, and he did visit England as a world-famous figure in 1931 — the setting the anecdote usually claims. That combination makes the story almost irresistible. But a line this quotable, delivered to reporters, would have been printed at the time, and it was not: the first trace is nineteen years after his death.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: We are careful here: you cannot prove a man never said something in an interview. What can be shown is that no record exists, that the first trace is nineteen years late, and that the joke was already circulating without him.

items.why: Gandhi died in January 1948. The earliest located attribution is January 1967, and it is narration on a television documentary, hedged as something he ‘was reported to have answered’ the trail ↗.
‘What’s your opinion of civilization?’ — ‘It’s a good idea. Somebody ought to start it’ ran as magazine filler in 1923. The gag needed only a famous mouth to put it in 1923 antecedent ↗.

Retellings specify a dockside press scrum on his 1931 England visit, or the palace. Those details have no source, and 1931 press coverage of Gandhi was extensive — the absence of any contemporaneous printing is itself meaningful.

misattribution.truthLine: No record before 1967, and the joke predates Gandhi by at least a quarter-century. Treat it as apocryphal — his real, sourced verdict on Western civilization is in Hind Swaraj (1909) citation trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The appeal is the manner as much as the content: a colonised man, asked a patronising question by the empire’s press, answering with a smile that costs them everything. It is the perfect anti-imperial punchline, which is precisely why it wants to be true.

What Gandhi actually wrote is less charming and more serious. In Hind Swaraj he treats modern civilization as an affliction — something the English are suffering from rather than something they have failed to begin.
detailsBody: 1923, Life filler: ‘What’s your opinion of civilization?’ ‘It’s a good idea. Somebody ought to start it.’
1925, newspaper variant: ‘The question is not where civilization began, but when will it.’
1948: Gandhi dies. No contemporaneous record of the exchange exists.
January 1967: a CBS documentary’s narration attaches it to Gandhi; press coverage repeats it, hedged.
Later 1967 onward: reprinted widely, the hedge dropped, settings invented.
context.pull: The joke was in print in 1923. Gandhi died in 1948. The attribution arrives in 1967.
